text: In 1980, a father-and-son team, the physicist Luis Alvarez and the [[geologist|geologist]] Walter Alvarez, reported something strange about a thin layer of clay near Gubbio in Italy. It was full of [[iridium|iridium]], a metal that is rare in [[@earth-layers-crust|Earth's crust]] but common in [[asteroid|asteroids]].

Then the same layer turned up all over the world, in rocks of the same age, about 66 million years old. Every clue pointed to one thing: an enormous impact from space. A decade later, the [[crater|crater]] itself was found, buried under Mexico.

spots: All over the world, rocks from 66 million years ago have one thin layer of clay. It's full of iridium, a metal that's rare on Earth's surface but common in asteroids.
Under a microscope, some sand grains in the layer have criss-cross scars. Only a gigantic impact can squeeze crystals that hard.
The impact melted rock and flung it into the sky. It rained back down as little glass beads, called spherules.
Dinosaur bones are found below the line. Above it, no non-bird dinosaur has ever been found.
In 1991 scientists confirmed a 180 km crater buried under Mexico, exactly the right age. The missing piece!

quiz.prompt: Walter Alvarez first tried to use the clay layer for a different job. What was he trying to measure?

options.t: How long the clay took to form
How much gold was in it
Whether dinosaurs ate clay

quiz.reveal: Space dust falls on Earth at a fairly steady rate, and it carries iridium. The team hoped the iridium would work like a clock. Instead they found far too much of it, as if a huge amount of space rock had arrived at once.

src: Alvarez L.W., Alvarez W., Asaro F. & Michel H.V. (1980) Extraterrestrial cause for the Cretaceous-Tertiary extinction. Science 208.
Hildebrand A.R. et al. (1991) Chicxulub Crater: A possible Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary impact crater on the Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico. Geology 19.
Alvarez W. (1997) T. rex and the Crater of Doom. Princeton University Press.

d.try: Make a layer cake of time in a clear glass. Pour in a layer of sand, then soil, then a thin sprinkle of cocoa or turmeric, then more sand. The thin coloured stripe is your boundary clay. Ask someone which layer went in first, and why they think so.
myth: Scientists decided an asteroid killed the dinosaurs because it seemed like an exciting story.
The idea was doubted for years. It won support slowly because evidence kept piling up from different places, ending with the crater found in Mexico in 1991.
facts: about 1–2 cm thick in many places

sec.t:
Walter Alvarez wanted to know how long the thin clay took to form. Tiny bits of space dust fall on Earth all the time, at a fairly steady rate, so the team thought iridium could work like a clock.

The clock broke. There was roughly 30 times more iridium than expected. Either the clay had taken an impossibly long time to settle, or a huge amount of space rock had arrived all at once. The team chose the second idea and suggested an asteroid about 10 km across. That is roughly the height of Mount Everest above sea level, as a single rock.

The big question was simple: if a huge rock hit, where is the hole? Much of Earth is ocean, and old seafloor slowly sinks back into the planet, so the crater might have vanished.

It hadn't. Geologists working for Mexico's oil company had noticed a giant ring buried under the Yucatán Peninsula years earlier. In 1991, Alan Hildebrand and his colleagues showed it was an [[@india-wonder-lonar|impact crater]] about 180 km wide, and the right age. It was named Chicxulub, after a village near its centre. Later dating has matched the crater and the clay layer very closely.

Below the clay, rocks contain the bones of non-bird dinosaurs, along with [[@ammonites|ammonites]] and other animals that vanished. Above it, none appear. Rocks are laid down one layer on top of another, a bit like newspapers piling up in a corner, so the clay marks a single moment in time. Scientists use the same idea of layers in [[@archaeology|archaeology]] and in working out the [[@fossil-age|age of fossils]].

Not every scientist thinks [[@extinction|the asteroid]] acted alone. Some argue the Deccan eruptions had already stressed life on Earth. But nearly all agree the impact was the main blow.

The boundary clay can be seen in many places: near Gubbio, and in the badlands of Montana and Colorado. In India, scientists found an iridium-rich layer between old [[lava|lava]] flows at Anjar in Kutch, Gujarat. In some spots you can put your finger on it. It looks like nothing much, just a pale or dark line in a cliff. It marks the moment the age of the dinosaurs ended.

text: A delta forms where a river flows into a sea or lake and slows down. A fast river can carry a lot of mud and sand. When it meets still water, it loses speed, and it can't carry its load any more. The [[sediment|sediment]] drops to the bottom and slowly builds new land.

As the land builds up, the river splits into many smaller channels, called [[distributary|distributaries]], which fan out across the new ground. Seen from above, many deltas look like a triangle or a fan, which is how they got their name.

st.prompt: Where does the word "delta" come from?

options.t: A letter of the Greek alphabet
The name of a river god
A Bengali word for island

st.reveal: The Greek letter delta is written Δ, a triangle. The Greek writer Herodotus noticed that the land at the mouth of the Nile spread out in the same triangle shape, and the name stuck for all river mouths like it.

src: United States Geological Survey (USGS), land area change in coastal Louisiana (2017).
Encyclopaedia Britannica, delta and Ganges-Brahmaputra delta.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, The Sundarbans and Sundarbans National Park.

d.try: Make a delta in a tray. Prop up one end of a baking tray on a book and spread a layer of damp sand at the top end. Slowly pour water from a jug onto the sand. Watch the water carve a little channel, then fan out and drop sand where it reaches the flat end. Keep pouring and the channel splits into branches.
myth: Every river makes a delta where it meets the sea.

A delta only forms where a river drops sand and mud faster than waves, tides and currents can carry it away. Some big rivers, like the Amazon, have strong tides and currents at their mouths and don't build a classic delta.
facts: mud and sand dropped where a river slows down
has lost about 4,800 sq km of land since 1932

sec.t:
Think of a river as a conveyor belt for sand and mud. The faster the water flows, the more it can carry. The Ganga and the Brahmaputra pick up enormous amounts of sediment from the young, crumbling mountains of the Himalaya.

When a river reaches the sea, its water spreads out and slows down. The biggest, heaviest grains drop first, close to the shore. Finer mud is carried farther out before it settles. Over time, these deposits build up into sandbanks, then islands, then solid land.

As sediment piles up in front of the river mouth, the river finds the main path blocked. It breaks through its banks and finds a new, lower route to the sea. Then that path fills up, and it shifts again.

So a delta is never finished. Its channels branch, wander and sometimes swap places over years and centuries. In big [[@floods-why|floods]], rivers can jump to a whole new course. People living on deltas have always had to live with water that moves.

The Nile delta in northern Egypt is the classic triangle that gave deltas their name. For thousands of years, the Nile's floods spread fresh mud across it. That made it some of the best farmland in the ancient world, as you can read in [[@egypt-nile|the Nile and ancient Egypt]].

The [[@mississippi|Mississippi]] delta, in Louisiana, has a different shape. Its channels stretch far into the Gulf of Mexico like the toes of a bird's foot. Scientists call it a bird's-foot delta.

Deltas need a steady supply of sediment to keep building. Dams trap mud upstream. Walls built along rivers to prevent floods also stop the mud from spreading over the land. Meanwhile, the soft delta ground slowly sinks under its own weight, and the [[@sea-level-rise|sea is rising]].

Louisiana has lost about 4,800 square kilometres of land since 1932, according to the US Geological Survey. In recent decades, it has lost on average about a football field of land every 100 minutes. In Egypt, the Aswan High Dam has cut off most of the Nile's mud from its delta.

Not every delta reaches the sea. In Botswana, the Okavango River flows into the Kalahari Desert and spreads out into a huge inland delta of channels, [[lagoon|lagoons]] and islands. The water never reaches an ocean. It soaks into the sand or evaporates. Every year the flood brings water to the desert, and elephants, hippos and countless birds follow it. In 2014, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

text: You can tell clouds apart by their shape and their height. There are three basic shapes. Heaps and puffs are called *cumulus*. Flat, grey layers are *stratus*. Thin, wispy streaks high up are *cirrus*. Add *nimbus*, meaning rain, and you have the building blocks of most cloud names.

Weather scientists group clouds into 10 main types, depending on these shapes and on whether they float low, in the middle or high in the sky. Each type forms in a different kind of air, so knowing your clouds can help you guess what the weather will do next.

st.prompt: About how much might an ordinary fluffy cumulus cloud weigh?

options.t: Less than a feather
About as much as a bicycle
About as much as a hundred elephants

st.reveal: A typical small cumulus cloud holds about 500 tonnes of water, spread through a huge space as tiny droplets. It floats because the droplets are so small and spread out, and because the rising air beneath it holds them up.

d.try: Keep a cloud diary for a week. Look at the sky at the same time each day, sketch the clouds, and try to name them using the three basic shapes, heaps, layers and wisps. Then write down what the weather did over the next few hours. Did the clouds give you a warning?
myth: Clouds are made of water vapour.
Water vapour is an invisible gas. Clouds are made of tiny drops of liquid water, or ice crystals, so small and light that rising air keeps them afloat. That's why you can see them.
facts: tiny water droplets or ice crystals
cumulonimbus, often more than 10 km tall

sec.h: The man who named the clouds
sec.t:
Before 1802, clouds had no widely used scientific names. Then a young English chemist named Luke Howard gave a talk in London. He suggested using [[@latin-roots|Latin words]] for their shapes: cumulus for heap, stratus for layer, cirrus for a curl of hair, and nimbus for rain cloud. You could combine them, so a rain-bringing layer became nimbostratus.

His idea caught on fast. The German writer Goethe even wrote poems in Howard's honour. Today the World Meteorological Organization keeps an official guide, the International Cloud Atlas, which still uses his names.

Low clouds sit below about 2 km. Stratus is a grey blanket that can hide hilltops. [[@fog-smog|Fog]] is simply a stratus cloud touching the ground. Fluffy cumulus clouds, the kind children draw, usually form on sunny days as warm air bubbles up from the ground.

Middle clouds float between about 2 and 7 km up. Altocumulus looks like rows of small puffs, sometimes called a mackerel sky.

High clouds, above about 6 km, are made of ice crystals. Cirrus looks like brushstrokes or horses' tails. A thin, milky sheet of cirrostratus can make a ring, or halo, around the Sun or Moon. Halos often show up a day or so before rain, as a weather system approaches.

{{story:clouds-rain}}

Cumulonimbus is the biggest cloud of all. It starts as a cumulus and keeps growing, sometimes to more than 10 km tall, higher than Mount Everest. At the top, it hits a layer of the air it can't rise through and spreads out flat, like the anvil of a blacksmith.

Inside, strong winds rush up and down. These clouds bring heavy rain, hail, [[@thunder-sound|thunder]] and [[@lightning|lightning]]. During India's [[@monsoon|monsoon]], towering cumulonimbus clouds build up over the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]] and the plains, and burst into downpours.

Clouds look weightless, but they hold a lot of water. Scientists have estimated that a small fluffy cumulus cloud contains around 500 tonnes of water, about the weight of a hundred elephants.

It doesn't fall because that water is split into billions of droplets, each far smaller than a grain of sand. They are so tiny that rising air holds them up. When the droplets bump together and grow too heavy, they fall as rain.

New kinds of clouds don't come along often. In 2017, the International Cloud Atlas added asperitas, a dark, rippled cloud base that looks like a rough sea seen from underneath. It was recognised partly thanks to photos sent in by members of the Cloud Appreciation Society from many countries.

Some clouds are made by people. The white lines behind high-flying jets are [[@sky-contrails|contrails]], clouds of ice crystals formed from water in the engine exhaust. On a cold, damp day they can spread out and become cirrus clouds. The same sky science feeds the computers behind [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]].

text: A glider flies the same way any plane does: air flowing over its wings creates [[lift|lift]]. But with no engine to push it forward, a glider must use [[gravity|gravity]]. It points slightly downhill through the air, trading height for speed, like a cyclist coasting down a long slope.

On its own, that would mean a slow, gentle trip to the ground. Glider pilots stay up by finding air that is rising faster than the glider is sinking. Warm air columns, wind pushed up over hills, and great waves of air behind mountains can all carry a glider upwards for hours.

st.prompt: A glider pilot has been flying for five hours without an engine. What has kept the glider up?

options.t: Columns of warm air rising from the ground
Air trapped inside its hollow wings
The speed it got from its launch

st.reveal: Sunshine heats patches of ground, and air above them rises in columns called thermals. A glider circles inside a thermal to gain height, then glides to the next one. On a good day this can go on for hours.

src: Federal Aviation Administration, Glider Flying Handbook.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Glider.
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, The Wright brothers and the invention of the aerial age.

d.try: Fold two paper planes of the same design, one with long, narrow wings and one with short, stubby wings. Launch each gently from the same height and see which glides farther before landing. Long, slender wings, like a real glider's, usually win.
myth: Without an engine, a glider will soon drop out of the sky.
Gliders are built to sink very slowly. In still air, a modern glider loses only about 1 m of height for every 40 to 60 m it travels forward. In rising air it can climb for thousands of metres.
facts: none (launched by a tow plane or winch)
over 50 km forward for every 1 km of height lost
over 3,000 km in a single day

sec.t:
Look at a modern glider and the first thing you notice is the wings. They are very long and very thin, sometimes over 25 m from tip to tip, longer than a cricket pitch. Long, slender wings make lift with very little [[drag|drag]], the air resistance that slows a plane down.

The body is smooth and narrow, and the pilot lies almost flat in a tight cockpit. The result is a machine that can travel more than 50 km forward for every kilometre of height it loses. A jumbo jet with its engines switched off manages about 15 to 20.

The sun does not heat the ground evenly. A ploughed field, a car park or a rocky hillside warms faster than a lake or a forest. Air above these warm patches rises in columns called thermals, often topped by a small, puffy cloud.

Birds found this out long before people. [[@vultures-india|Vultures]] and kites rarely flap once they are high above an Indian city. They spiral inside thermals, then glide off in search of the next. Glider pilots do exactly the same, watching for circling birds and new clouds. A small instrument called a variometer beeps faster as the glider rises, so the pilot can feel the edges of a thermal without looking down.

Wind blowing against a ridge is forced upwards too. When strong [[@wind-blows|wind]] crosses a mountain range, it can set up huge invisible waves of air behind it, reaching far higher than any thermal.

{{story:wright-brothers}}

In the 1890s, the German engineer Otto Lilienthal made around 2,000 flights in gliders he built himself, running down hills near Berlin. His work inspired two bicycle makers from Ohio. Between 1900 and 1902, the [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]] flew gliders over the sand dunes of [[@wright-to-moon|Kitty Hawk]], North Carolina, learning how to steer and balance. Only then did they add an engine in 1903.

In 2018, the Perlan 2 glider rode mountain waves over the Andes in Argentina to about 23 km. That is roughly twice the height at which [[@airplanes-fly|airliners]] usually cruise. The two pilots wore pressure suits, like astronauts, because the air up there is far too thin to breathe.

Every plane can glide, even huge ones. In 1983, an Air Canada Boeing 767 ran out of fuel at 12 km after a mix-up between pounds and kilograms. The crew glided it to a former air force base at Gimli, Manitoba, and everyone on board survived. The plane became known as the Gimli Glider.

The American space shuttle landed as a glider too. It had no engines for landing, so it came in steeply from space and had a single chance to touch down. Pilots practised in special training jets set up to fly like the shuttle, gliding down again and again until the steep approach felt normal.

text: Owls turn their heads so far because they can't move their eyes. An owl's eyes are huge for its body, and to fit in the skull they grew long and tube-shaped, like a pair of binoculars. A ring of bone inside each eye holds it firmly in place.

So when an owl wants to look to the side or behind, it turns its whole head. Its neck is built for this. It has twice as many neck bones as yours, and blood vessels with clever safety features, letting it turn its head up to about 270 degrees without harm.

st.prompt: How far can an owl turn its head in one direction?

options.t: About three-quarters of a full circle
All the way round, a full circle
About the same as a person

st.reveal: Owls can turn their heads up to about 270 degrees, three-quarters of a circle. Turning one way and then the other lets them see behind them so smoothly that it can look like a full circle.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Owl.
de Kok-Mercado F. et al. (2013) Adaptations of the owl's cervical and cephalic arteries in relation to extreme neck rotation. Science 339.
Payne R.S. (1971) Acoustic location of prey by barn owls. Journal of Experimental Biology 54.

d.try: Keep your head still and look as far left as you can using only your eyes. Now pretend your eyes are glued in place. Ask a friend to stand behind you and hold up some fingers, and see how far you have to turn your head and body to count them. That is an owl's problem every time it wants to look around.
myth: Owls can turn their heads all the way round in a full circle.
They can't. The limit is about 270 degrees in each direction. That is still far more than a person can manage, which is about 90 degrees.
facts: can catch mice by sound alone

sec.t:
Most animals' eyes are round balls that roll in their sockets. An owl's eyes are long and narrow, with a big lens at the front. That shape lets a lot of light fall onto the [[retina|retina]], which helps owls see in dim light. In some owls the eyes take up more room in the skull than the brain does.

Both eyes face forward, like ours. This gives owls very good depth perception, the ability to judge exactly how far away a mouse is before pouncing. The cost is a narrower view. To make up for it, owls bob, tilt and swivel their heads constantly.

Your neck has 7 small bones called vertebrae. An owl has 14. More joints mean more ways to bend and twist.

There is a second problem. If you twisted your neck sharply, you could squeeze the blood vessels that feed your brain. In 2013, a team at Johns Hopkins University in the United States studied owls that had died of natural causes. They injected dye into the blood vessels and took scans. They found that an owl's main neck [[artery|arteries]] run through wide bony tunnels with room to spare. Near the head, the vessels widen into small pools that store extra blood while the neck is twisted.

Owls live on every continent except Antarctica. In India, the spotted owlet often roosts in city trees, and the large Indian eagle-owl hunts on rocky hills. In the United States, the great horned owl lives everywhere from deserts to big-city parks.

People have told stories about owls for thousands of years. In ancient Athens, the little owl was linked to Athena, goddess of wisdom. In Hindu tradition, the owl is the vehicle of Lakshmi, goddess of wealth. Sadly, false beliefs about owl magic still lead to some being caught and sold illegally around festivals in India, which conservation groups are working to stop. Owls are protected by law in both India and the United States, and the best place to meet one is in the wild, as one of many [[@nocturnal-animals|animals of the night]].

text: A matchstick is a thin splint of wood or waxed cardboard with a blob of chemicals on one end. In a factory, a machine slices soft wood into thin sheets, then chops the sheets into tiny sticks. The sticks are soaked in a chemical so they don't keep glowing after they're blown out, then dried.

Next, a machine holds thousands of sticks in rows of holes on a moving belt. It dips their tips into melted wax, so the flame catches the wood, and then into a paste that forms the head. The heads dry, the sticks are pushed out into boxes, and the boxes get a strip on the side. A single big machine can make millions of matches a day.

st.prompt: Where is the red phosphorus in a box of safety matches?

options.t: On the brown strip on the side of the box
In the red tip of the match
Inside the wooden stick

st.reveal: The red phosphorus is on the striking strip. Rubbing the match head against it makes a tiny bit of phosphorus flare up, which lights the chemicals in the head. That's why a safety match won't light on most other surfaces.

Royal Society of Chemistry, the chemistry of matches.

d.try: Rub your palms together fast for ten seconds, then hold them against your cheeks. Feel the warmth? That is friction turning movement into heat, the same start a match needs. Try it with dry hands and then with soapy wet hands and compare.
myth: The red tip of a safety match is made of red phosphorus.
The colour on the tip is usually just a dye. The red phosphorus is on the striking strip of the box. Keeping the two apart is what makes safety matches safer.
facts: invented in Sweden in the 1840s, mass-produced from the 1850s
mainly potassium chlorate, sulphur, glue and powdered glass
the Sivakasi and Kovilpatti area of Tamil Nadu

sec.t:
Before matches, lighting a fire meant rubbing sticks, striking flint against steel or carrying hot coals around. Early chemical matches were dangerous: some had to be dipped into a little bottle of [[acid|acid]].

In 1826, an English chemist named John Walker was mixing chemicals with a stick. A blob dried on its tip. When he scraped it across the floor, it burst into flame. In 1827 he began selling "[[friction|friction]] lights" in his shop, to be pulled through a fold of sandpaper. It was a classic [[@inventions-accidents|accidental invention]].

In the 1840s, a Swedish chemist found a safer idea: split the chemicals in two. The head carries potassium chlorate, which gives off oxygen when heated, plus sulphur and glue. The box strip carries red phosphorus and powdered glass.

When you strike, [[@friction|friction]] heats a tiny bit of red phosphorus, which flares and lights the head. The potassium chlorate feeds oxygen to the sulphur, which catches, then the wax, then the wood. All of this happens in about a second. Swedish factories made safety matches famous around the world from the 1850s.

Most of India's matches come from a small area of Tamil Nadu around Sivakasi, Kovilpatti and Sattur. The hot, dry [[climate|climate]] is good for drying matches. The industry grew in the 1920s, when local businessmen learned the trade and set up factories.

Sivakasi is also famous for fireworks and printing. For many years, children worked in its match factories, filling boxes by hand. Laws, inspections and campaigns have greatly reduced this, and it is now illegal for children to work there. The wider problem is covered in the story of [[@child-labour|child labour]].

Many match factories now use machines, though some smaller units still do steps like filling boxes by hand.

A box of matches still costs very little in India. In 2021 the usual price rose from 1 rupee to 2 rupees, the first change in 14 years. Matches remain important for cooking stoves, lamps and festivals.

Lighters have replaced matches in many places, but a match never runs out of gas and needs no spare parts. They are tools, not toys, and only an adult should strike them, which is a key rule of [[@kitchen-safety|kitchen safety]].

text: Building a road starts with the ground. Workers scrape away soft soil and plants, then flatten and squash the earth underneath with heavy rollers until it is firm. This is called the subgrade.

On top go layers of crushed stone, coarse at the bottom and finer above. Each layer is spread and rolled hard, so the stones lock together and spread the weight of traffic over a wide area. Finally comes the surface. Most roads are topped with asphalt, small stones mixed with hot, sticky black bitumen. It is spread by a paving machine and pressed smooth by rollers while it is still hot. Some roads are topped with concrete instead. Concrete roads cost more to build but can last much longer, so they are often used on busy [[@fastag-tolls|highways and expressways]].
The top is shaped slightly higher in the middle than at the edges, so rain runs off into drains.

options.t: Water getting under the road surface
Heavy trucks alone
Hot sunshine melting the road

st.reveal: Water seeps through small cracks and softens the layers underneath. Traffic then presses the weak spot until it breaks apart. In cold places, water freezes in the cracks and expands, pushing them wider. Heavy traffic makes it worse, but water starts the damage.

d.try: Build a road in a clear plastic cup. Put a layer of soil at the bottom and press it down, then a layer of small pebbles, then a layer of sand, pressing each one firm. Slowly pour a little water on top and watch where it goes. Try another cup with only soil and compare.
myth: Potholes are caused only by heavy trucks.

Trucks do add stress, but water is the real villain. It seeps under the surface, weakens the layers below and, in cold places, freezes and cracks the road from inside. Good drainage is one of the most important parts of any road.

sec.h: The Romans and Grand Trunk Road
sec.t:
People have built roads for thousands of years. The Romans laid more than 80,000 kilometres of paved roads across their [[empire|empire]], with deep layers of stones and a curved top for drainage. Some [[@roman-roads|Roman roads]] are still in use.

In South Asia, a great road has run across the north for well over 2,000 years. In the 1500s, the ruler Sher Shah Suri rebuilt it with rest houses and trees along the way. Under British rule it became known as the Grand Trunk Road. Today, parts of it run from Bangladesh through [[@pakistan-history|India and Pakistan]] into Afghanistan.

In the USA, it wasn't drivers who first demanded better roads. In the 1880s and 1890s, cyclists formed clubs that campaigned for smooth paved roads, in what became known as the Good Roads Movement. When cars arrived soon after, the roads were partly ready for them.

Every road eventually wears out. Water seeps through cracks and softens the layers below. Traffic pounds the weak spot, and a pothole opens. In [[@cold-places|cold places]] like the northern USA, water freezes and expands inside cracks, breaking roads apart each winter. In India, heavy [[monsoon|monsoon]] rains do similar damage.

In the early 2000s, Rajagopalan Vasudevan, a chemistry professor in Madurai, Tamil Nadu, found a use for waste [[@plastic-made|plastic]] bags. Shredded and melted into hot bitumen, the plastic helped bind the stones and keep water out. His method has since been used to build thousands of kilometres of roads in India.

Engineers elsewhere are trying [[@tyres|old car tyres]], crushed glass and recycled asphalt scraped up from worn-out roads. India now has one of the largest road networks in the world, over 60 lakh kilometres, and finding cheap, tough materials to build and fix it is a big task.

text: Banarasi silk is famous for its brocade: patterns of shining metallic thread woven right into the silk, so they look embroidered but are part of the cloth itself. Flowers, vines, birds and paisleys seem to float on the fabric. The best pieces use zari, fine silver wire coated in gold.

These saris come from Varanasi, also called Banaras, and the districts around it. [[weaving|Weaving]] them takes great skill and a lot of time. That's why a Banarasi sari is often bought for a wedding and then passed from mother to daughter for generations.

st.prompt: Long before computers, Banarasi weavers used punched cards to control their looms. What did the holes in the cards decide?

options.t: Which threads were lifted to make the pattern
How fast the loom moved
What colour the silk was dyed

st.reveal: On a Jacquard loom, each hole lets a hook lift one warp thread. A chain of cards spells out a pattern row by row. The same idea of holes and no holes later helped inspire early computers.

src: Ministry of Textiles, Government of India, handloom clusters of Varanasi.

d.try: Make a paper weave. Cut slits in a sheet of coloured paper, leaving a border, then weave strips of another colour over and under. Try changing the pattern, such as over two and under one, and see what new designs appear.
myth: Every Banarasi sari is handwoven with real gold thread.
Many saris sold as Banarasi today are made on power looms with plastic-based metallic thread. A genuine handwoven sari from the GI area can carry a Banaras Brocades GI tag.
facts: Varanasi and nearby districts, Uttar Pradesh
silver wire coated with gold, or cheaper copper and polyester today
kadhua, where each motif is woven separately by hand

sec.t:
To make traditional zari, craftspeople pulled silver through smaller and smaller holes until it became a wire thinner than a human hair. They flattened it, coated it with gold and wound it around a silk core. Today most zari is made with copper, or even plastic film coated to look like metal, which costs far less.

Old pieces made with real zari were so valuable that families sometimes burned worn-out saris to recover the silver and gold. Museums like the Victoria and Albert in London keep Banarasi brocades in their collections.

sec.h: Weaving a picture, one thread at a time

sec.t:
The most prized technique is called *kadhua*. Each [[motif|motif]], such as a small flower called a *buta*, is woven separately with its own little bobbin of thread, by hand. On the back of the cloth, there are no loose threads hanging across. It is slow, careful work.

In cheaper *phekwa* weaving, the extra thread runs right across the back of the fabric and the loose parts are cut off later. Turn a sari over, and an expert can tell you how it was made in seconds.

Silk weaving in Varanasi goes back many centuries, but the gold-heavy style people picture today grew in the time of the [[@mughals|Mughals]]. Persian designs like the *jaal*, a net of vines, and the *kalga*, a paisley shape, mixed with Indian flowers and temple patterns.

Most weavers work in family workshops in neighbourhoods of [[@varanasi|Varanasi]], many from Muslim Ansari families, while many traders and buyers are Hindu. Banarasi silk links both communities, and the saris are worn at weddings and festivals of every faith.

Weaving by hand is hard to make a living from. A power loom can turn out a sari in hours, and cheap copies flood the markets. Many young people from weaving families have left for other jobs.

In 2009, the government gave "Banaras Brocades and Sarees" a Geographical Indication tag. That means only cloth from the Varanasi area, made in the traditional way, can legally use the name. Some weavers now sell directly online, and designers have brought Banarasi brocade into jackets, lehengas and even sneakers.

Silk isn't the only Indian fibre with a story. Far to the north, in the cold Himalaya, goats grow a winter coat so fine it becomes [[@art-pashmina|pashmina]].

text: Open a school bag in Chennai, Chicago, Tokyo or Nairobi and you'll find a lot of the same things: books, a pencil box, a water bottle, something to eat. But the bags themselves, and how heavy they are, can be very different.

Some children carry hard leather boxes on their backs. Some pull wheeled trolleys like tiny airline passengers. Some carry a light cloth bag with a single slate. And some carry so much that governments have made rules about it, including India's [[@schools-world|School Bag Policy]] of 2020.

st.prompt: India's School Bag Policy says a bag should weigh no more than what share of a child's body weight?

options.t: About a tenth
About a quarter
About half

st.reveal: The 2020 policy says around 10%. So a child who weighs 30 kg should carry a bag of about 3 kg or less. Many surveys found kids carrying far more than that.

src: Ministry of Education, Government of India, School Bag Policy 2020.
American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org, backpack safety.

d.try: Weigh yourself on a bathroom scale, then weigh yourself again holding your packed school bag. The difference is the weight of your bag. Divide it by your own weight and multiply by 100 to find the percentage. Is it under 10? If not, see what you can leave at home.
myth: Carrying a heavy school bag gives children a permanently curved spine.

Studies have not shown that heavy bags cause scoliosis, a sideways curve of the spine. Heavy or badly worn bags can still cause back and shoulder pain, so lighter bags carried on both shoulders are better.
facts: hard box-shaped bag, used for all six years of primary school
bag should weigh no more than about 10% of the child's body weight
a backpack should be under 10–20% of body weight
common in parts of Europe and China

sec.t:
In Japan, almost every primary school child wears a randoseru. It is a stiff, box-shaped backpack, usually made of leather or tough synthetic leather. Families often buy one just before the first year of school, and it is expected to last all six years. A good one can cost around as much as a bicycle.

The idea came from the Netherlands. In the 1800s, Japan borrowed a Dutch soldier's backpack called a *ransel*, and the name drifted into randoseru. The hard shape protects books, and some families say it can even cushion a child who falls backwards. Plenty of Japanese adults keep their old randoseru as a souvenir, and some send them to children in other countries.

In India, school bags have long been famous for being heavy. Textbooks, notebooks for every subject, a steel tiffin, a water bottle, sometimes sports kit: it adds up. Surveys in Indian cities have found young children carrying bags that weighed a quarter or more of their own body weight.

So in 2020, India's Ministry of Education issued a School Bag Policy. It says a bag should weigh about 10% of a child's body weight. Schools are asked to keep lockers, plan timetables so fewer books come each day, and give no homework to Classes 1 and 2. Some schools now weigh bags at the gate.

Lunch is its own story. In Mumbai, many office workers don't even carry their lunch: [[@lunchbox-dabbawala|dabbawalas]] bring it to them. Children mostly still carry their own.

{{story:lunchbox-dabbawala}}

In parts of Europe and China, many children drag wheeled bags. They save shoulders but bump down stairs, and some schools have banned them to stop children tripping in corridors.

In the United States, the zipped nylon backpack rules. It became common in the 1970s and 1980s, when companies began selling light outdoor packs to students. Doctors there often suggest a bag should be under 10–20% of body weight, worn on both shoulders, with the heaviest things packed closest to the back.

In many villages around the world, children still carry very little. A cloth bag, a notebook, perhaps a slate and chalk. A slate weighs little, and the same one can be wiped and used for years, which makes it one of the cheapest school tools ever made.

sec.h: What the bag says about school
sec.t:
What children carry tells you about how their school works. Lots of books means lots of subjects taught from textbooks. Lockers mean the school expects things to stay there. A tablet in the bag means digital lessons.

Even the water bottle tells a story. Not long ago, many children drank from a school tap or a shared pot. Now the plastic or steel [[@water-bottle|water bottle]] is in nearly every bag on Earth. And the strangest part is how much all that kit weighs in the end, which comes down to the simple maths of [[@weights-mass|weight and mass]].

text: School looks different around the world, but its main aims are much the same: to teach children to read, write and count, to understand the world, and to get along with others. What changes is when school starts, how long the day lasts, what children wear and eat, how they learn and how they are tested.

In some countries, children begin formal lessons at five. In Finland they wait until seven. Some children walk to school, some ride buses, some take boats, and a few go to school over the internet from homes hundreds of kilometres from the nearest classroom.

st.prompt: In Japan, who usually cleans the classroom at the end of the school day?

options.t: The students
Paid cleaners
Parents, taking turns

st.reveal: Japanese students take turns sweeping floors, wiping desks and cleaning shared areas in a daily cleaning time. Many students also serve lunch to their classmates. The idea is that everyone takes care of the place they share.

src: OECD, Education at a Glance.
Finnish National Agency for Education.
Ministry of Education, Government of India, PM POSHAN scheme.

d.try: Write a timetable for your ideal school day, then compare it with a classmate's. Next, look up the school timetable of a child in another country with an adult's help. Which ideas from that country would you borrow for your own school?
myth: Finland's schools have no homework and no tests.
Finnish students do get homework, usually less than in many countries, and teachers test them in class. What Finland mostly avoids is national exams before the end of upper secondary school.
facts: Australia's School of the Air began
Children fed by India's school meal scheme
Solar-powered boat schools in Bangladesh began

sec.t:
In Japan, the school year starts in April, when cherry trees blossom. Students take turns serving lunch to their classmates, often wearing white coats and caps. After lunch or at the end of the day, everyone cleans: sweeping, mopping, wiping windows and scrubbing sinks. Teachers say it teaches responsibility and respect for shared spaces.

{{story:japan-culture}}

Finnish children usually start formal school at seven, after a year of preschool. School days are fairly short, there are breaks between lessons for outdoor play, and students typically get less homework than in many countries. Teachers need a master's degree and are given a lot of freedom. Finland became famous after its students scored very well in international tests in the early 2000s.

In the Australian outback, some families live on cattle stations far from any town. Since 1951, their children have attended [[@australia|School of the Air]], starting in Alice Springs. Students first used two-way [[@radio-waves|radios]] to talk to teachers and classmates hundreds of kilometres away. Today they use the internet and [[@tech-video-calls|video calls]], and they meet in person a few times a year.

In parts of [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]], [[monsoon|monsoon]] [[@floods-why|floods]] cut villages off for months. Since 2002, an organisation called Shidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha has run boat schools. Solar-powered boats pick children up from their villages, hold lessons on board, and drop them home again.

India has one of the largest school systems in the world, with crores of students in government and private schools. The school year usually begins in April or June, depending on the state. Many students wear uniforms, and board exams at the end of Classes 10 and 12 are big events in family life.

Under the PM POSHAN scheme, often still called the [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]], about 11 crore children in government schools (2025 figure) get a free cooked lunch each school day. Studies have found it helps attendance, especially among girls.

[[@life-kids-around-world|Children around the world]] learn in many languages. In India, many students learn in their mother tongue, Hindi and English, often all three. In the United States, most public schools do not require uniforms, and the school year usually starts in August or September. In France, [[@lunch-world|school lunches]] are often several courses, with a starter, a main dish, cheese and a dessert.

Exams differ too. In China and [[@seoul|South Korea]], a single university entrance exam can shape a student's future, and many go to extra classes in the evenings. Each system has supporters and critics. Comparing them helps educators borrow good ideas from each other, as [[@school-history|the history of school]] shows they always have.

text: The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, or IMF, are two global institutions set up after the Second World War. They are owned by their member countries, about 190 of them, including India and the USA.

The World Bank lends money and gives advice to developing countries for long-term projects, such as roads, dams, schools, hospitals and clean water. The IMF has a different job. It watches over the world's money system and lends to countries that run into a sudden crisis, for example when they can't pay for [[import|imports]] or repay foreign debts. You could think of the World Bank as a builder and the IMF as a firefighter.

st.prompt: By tradition, which countries have chosen the heads of the World Bank and the IMF?

options.t: The USA for the World Bank, and Europe for the IMF
India for both
A lottery among all members

st.reveal: Since the 1940s, the World Bank president has always been American and the IMF head has always been European. Many developing countries, including India, have argued that the top jobs should be open to the best candidate from anywhere.

src: International Monetary Fund (imf.org), history of the IMF.
World Bank Group (worldbank.org), history and archives.
Reserve Bank of India, the 1991 balance of payments crisis (RBI history volumes).
n.certNote: What the two institutions do is well documented. Whether the conditions they attach to loans have helped or hurt poorer countries is strongly debated by economists and governments.

d.try: Play a lending game with friends and pretend coins. One person is the "bank" with 20 coins. Two others each borrow 5 to start a pretend stall, promising to pay back 6 later. Decide what the bank should do if one stall fails. Should it lend again, forgive the debt or demand changes first?
myth: The World Bank is a bank where ordinary people can open an account.
The World Bank lends to governments, not to individuals. It raises money from member countries and by selling bonds, then lends it for things like roads, schools, clean water and power.
facts: Bretton Woods conference, New Hampshire, July 1944

sec.h: Born in a hotel in the mountains

sec.t:
The World Bank's first loan, in 1947, went to France for rebuilding after the war. Soon it turned to poorer countries. In 1949, India received its first World Bank loan, for its [[@indian-railways|railways]]. Since then, India has been one of the bank's biggest borrowers, for projects from power plants to rural roads and school programmes.

The bank raises money by selling bonds and from its member countries. Its poorest borrowers get loans at very low or no [[@money-interest-loans|interest]], with decades to repay, and sometimes grants that don't need paying back.

By 1991, India was in deep trouble. Oil prices had jumped, and it had foreign money left for only a few weeks of imports. To borrow, the government sent tonnes of the country's gold to the Bank of England as security.

India also borrowed from the IMF. Some of the changes that followed were conditions of the loans, and many were ones the new government wanted anyway. The government cut many controls on business, lowered taxes on imports and opened up to [[@global-companies|foreign companies]]. [[@economic-reforms-1991|These reforms]], led by Finance Minister Manmohan Singh, helped [[@india-economy|India's economy]] grow much faster over the following decades.

IMF loans usually come with conditions, such as cutting government spending, raising taxes or selling state companies. Supporters say these steps fix the problems that caused the crisis. Critics argue that, in some countries, they led to job losses and cuts to health and education, hurting the poorest people.

There are also arguments about power. Votes in both institutions depend largely on how much money a country puts in, so the USA and Europe have the most say. By tradition, an American leads the World Bank and a European leads the IMF. Many developing countries, including India, want a bigger voice. Over the years, both bodies have shifted voting shares slightly. They now also talk more about reducing poverty and tackling [[climate|climate]] change, alongside their old worries about debt and [[@inflation|inflation]].

text: Speed tells you how far something goes in a certain amount of time. To work it out, divide the distance by the time.
If a bus travels 60 km in 2 hours, its speed is 60 ÷ 2 = 30 km per hour. If you walk 100 metres in 50 seconds, your speed is 100 ÷ 50 = 2 metres per second.

You can turn the formula around too. Distance equals speed times time. Time equals distance divided by speed. If you know any two of the three, you can find the third. That's how a train timetable is made, and how a map app guesses when you'll arrive.

st.prompt: You see lightning, then count 6 seconds before you hear the thunder. Roughly how far away was the lightning?

options.t: About 200 metres
About 2 kilometres
About 20 kilometres

st.reveal: Light reaches you almost instantly, but sound travels about 343 metres each second. In 6 seconds that's about 2,000 metres, or 2 km. A handy rule is to divide the seconds by 3 to get kilometres.

src: World Athletics, world records.
NASA, International Space Station facts and figures.

d.try: Measure out 20 metres in a park or playground with a grown-up. Time a friend walking it, then running it. Work out each speed by dividing 20 by the number of seconds. Multiply by 3.6 to change metres per second into kilometres per hour.
myth: You can't feel the Earth moving because it moves slowly.

The Earth moves very fast, both spinning and travelling round the Sun. You don't feel it because the motion is smooth and steady, and you, the air and everything around you move along together. We only feel changes in speed, not speed itself.

sec.t:
The speed you work out this way is an average. A bus that covers 30 km in an hour probably didn't go 30 km/h the whole time. It stopped at signals, crawled in traffic and sped up on open road. The number on its speedometer at any moment is its speed at that instant.

[[@usain-bolt|Usain Bolt]] ran 100 metres in 9.58 seconds at the World Championships in Berlin in 2009. That's an average of about 10.4 metres per second, or about 37.6 km/h. But he started from standing still. In the fastest part of the race, he reached nearly 45 km/h.

Speed can be measured in many units. Cars and trains in India use kilometres per hour. Cars in the United States use miles per hour. Scientists often use metres per second. Ships and planes use knots, which are nautical miles per hour.

To change metres per second into kilometres per hour, multiply by 3.6. That works because an hour has 3,600 seconds and a kilometre has 1,000 metres. So a sprinter at 10 m/s is going 36 km/h.

[[@what-if-earth-stopped|The Earth spins once a day]]. At the [[equator|equator]], the ground travels about 40,000 km in 24 hours, which is about 1,670 km/h. In Bengaluru it's a little less, and at the poles almost zero.

At the same time, the Earth travels round the Sun at about 1,07,000 km/h. You don't feel any of this, because the motion is smooth and you move along with it. You only notice changes in speed, like a train braking suddenly.

The [[@space-station|International Space Station]] circles the Earth at about 28,000 km/h, roughly 7.7 km every second. At that speed it goes all the way round in about 90 minutes. Astronauts on board see about 16 sunrises and sunsets every day.

Space probes go faster still. The fastest, NASA's Parker Solar Probe, has flown past the Sun at more than 6 lakh km/h. Even at that speed, it would take about nine days to cross the distance from the Earth to the Sun.

Marathon runners use the same maths as space scientists. A runner who wants to finish the 42.195 km of a [[@running-marathon|marathon]] in 3 hours must average about 14 km/h the whole way.

text: Basketball was invented in December 1891 by James Naismith, a Canadian physical education teacher at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, in the United States. His boss asked him to create an indoor game that would keep young men active through the long, snowy New England winter.

Naismith wrote 13 rules, hung two peach baskets from a balcony and gave his class a [[@football-world|football]] to throw. Within a few years the game had spread across America. Today it is one of the most played sports on Earth.

st.prompt: In the very first game of basketball, how did the players get the ball back after each score?

options.t: Someone climbed up and took it out of the peach basket
It dropped through a hole in the net
A new ball was thrown in from the side

st.reveal: The peach baskets still had their bottoms, so someone had to fetch the ball after every basket. Open-bottomed nets came later, which is why the game sped up.

d.try: Set up a waste-paper basket on a chair and stand two big steps back. Try ten throws with a rolled-up sock ball using an overhead push, then ten with an underarm lob. Count which style scores more, and why a high arc might help.
myth: Basketball was invented by an American.
James Naismith was born in Canada, in Ontario. He invented the game while working in the United States and became a US citizen only in 1925.
facts: YMCA training school, Springfield, Massachusetts, USA

sec.t:
Winter in Massachusetts is cold and dark, and Naismith's students were tired of marching drills and [[@gymnastics|gymnastics]]. They were rough, restless and bored. Naismith had about two weeks to come up with something better.

He wanted a game that was safe indoors, so no tackling. He wanted skill to matter more than strength. So he decided the goal should be high above the players' heads, where nobody could guard it by standing in front of it. A ball would have to be thrown in an arc, which takes aim, not force.

Naismith had 18 students, so the first game was nine against nine. Players could not run with the ball, and there was no dribbling yet. They could only pass. After a long struggle, a student named William Chase landed the only basket. The game ended 1–0.

Someone had to climb up to retrieve the ball whenever a shot went in. Metal hoops with open nets replaced the baskets over the following years. Dribbling, the backboard and the five-a-side team all came later.

Naismith's students went home for [[@christmas|Christmas]] and took the game with them. YMCAs across the United States and [[@canada|Canada]], and soon in other countries, began to play it.

Women started almost at once. In 1892 Senda Berenson, a teacher at Smith College in Massachusetts, adapted the rules for her students. Basketball joined the [[@olympics|Olympics]] in Berlin in 1936, and Naismith, by then in his seventies, was there to see it. The professional league that became the NBA began in 1946.

Basketball reached India in the early 20th century, carried partly by the YMCA, the same organisation that ran Naismith's school. Today it is played in schools and colleges across the country, on cement courts as often as wooden ones.

In 2015 Satnam Singh Bhamara, from a village in Punjab, became the first Indian-born player chosen in the NBA draft.

Modern players train with [[@sports-science|sports scientists]] who measure jump height, shooting angles and sleep. Coaches have learned that a high, arcing shot gives the ball a bigger target to fall into, which is exactly what Naismith's high basket was meant to reward.

Naismith himself never made money from his game. He spent most of his career teaching at the University of Kansas, where he coached the basketball team. He is one of the very few coaches in the school's history with more losses than wins.

text: The first video games were made by scientists, not game companies. In 1958, a physicist named William Higinbotham built Tennis for Two for a visitors' day at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York. Two players turned knobs to hit a glowing dot over a net on a small round screen. Visitors queued to play it, but after a second open day in 1959 it was taken apart.

In 1962, students at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) made Spacewar!, in which two spaceships fought around a star. Ten years later, games left the lab. The Magnavox Odyssey plugged into home televisions, and Pong filled arcades. From there it took only a few years for games to become a business worth billions.

st.prompt: In 1958, what screen did people use to play Tennis for Two?

options.t: A round screen on a machine called an oscilloscope
A black-and-white television
A cinema screen at a science fair

st.reveal: Tennis for Two ran on a small round oscilloscope screen, a lab instrument for showing electrical signals. The "ball" was a bright dot that bounced over a line for a net.

The Strong National Museum of Play, World Video Game Hall of Fame.
n.certNote: Historians argue about which game counts as the first, because it depends on what you call a video game. Tennis for Two (1958), Spacewar (1962) and the first home console (1972) all have a claim.

d.try: Play "paper Pong" with a friend. Draw a court on a sheet of paper, put a coin in the middle, and take turns flicking it toward each other's goal line with one finger. Then think about which rules a computer would need to know to run the same game.
myth: Video games were invented by toy companies to sell to children.

The earliest games were made by scientists and university students on huge, expensive machines, mostly for fun and to show what computers could do. Toy and arcade companies came later, once the machines got cheaper.
facts: 1962, on a PDP-1 computer at MIT

sec.h: The brown box that came home
sec.t:
In the 1960s, an engineer named Ralph Baer had an idea: millions of homes already had a television, so why not play games on it? His team built a test machine nicknamed the Brown Box. It became the Magnavox Odyssey, sold in 1972 as the [[@tech-game-consoles|first home video game console]].

The Odyssey could only draw a few white squares and a line. To add colour, it came with plastic sheets you stuck on the TV screen. The Brown Box is now kept at the Smithsonian in Washington, DC.

Also in 1972, a new company called Atari put Pong in a bar in California. It was a simple [[@table-tennis|table tennis]] game, but people loved it. Within a few years, arcades with rows of coin-operated machines opened across the USA and Japan.

In 1978, the Japanese company Taito released Space Invaders, with rows of aliens marching down the screen. Pac-Man followed in 1980. Its designer, Toru Iwatani, wanted a game that would appeal to everyone, including people who didn't like shooting games.

By 1983, shops in North America were flooded with too many poor games, and sales collapsed. Many people thought video games were a passing craze.

Then the Japanese company Nintendo brought its Famicom console to America in 1985, renamed the Nintendo Entertainment System, along with Super Mario Bros. Sales recovered. In 1989 came the Game Boy, with the puzzle game Tetris, first written in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov in Moscow.

Few Indian homes had game consoles in the 1980s. In the 1990s, many Indian children played cheap copies of the Nintendo Famicom, sold in local markets as "TV games" with cartridges holding dozens of games. Others played handheld brick games at school breaks.

Today India has one of the largest numbers of gamers anywhere, mostly playing on phones. Every one of those games still uses the same basic trick as Tennis for Two: a screen made of [[@pixels|pixels]], a computer following rules, and a player trying to beat them.

text: You see clearly when light entering your eye is focused sharply on the [[retina|retina]], the light-sensing layer at the back. The [[cornea|cornea]] at the front and the lens just behind it do the focusing, a bit like the lens in a camera.

If the eye is a little too long or too short, or if the cornea is curved unevenly, the light focuses in the wrong place and the picture is blurry. Glasses add an extra lens in front of the eye that bends the light by just the right amount, so the image lands sharply on the retina again. Doctors call these focusing problems refractive errors, and they are very common.

st.prompt: In a short-sighted eye, where does light from a faraway object come into focus?

options.t: Just in front of the retina
Exactly on the retina
Behind the eye

st.reveal: In a short-sighted eye, the eyeball is usually a little too long, so the image focuses before it reaches the retina and looks blurry. A lens that is thinner in the middle spreads the light slightly so it focuses in the right place.

src: Holden B. A. et al. (2016) Global prevalence of myopia and high myopia and temporal trends from 2000 through 2050. Ophthalmology.

d.try: Fill a clear, smooth glass with water and look at a printed page through it from the side. Move it closer and further away. The curved water acts like a lens and makes the letters bigger, smaller or upside down, just like the lenses used in glasses.
myth: Reading in dim light or sitting close to the TV will permanently damage your eyes.

These can tire your eyes and give you a headache, but there's no good evidence they cause lasting damage. Children often sit close to screens because they can focus up close easily, or because they are short-sighted and need an eye test.
facts: close things are harder to focus on

sec.t:
In short-sightedness, or myopia, the eyeball is usually slightly too long. Nearby things look clear, but the board at school or a bus number looks fuzzy. Glasses with lenses thinner in the middle fix it.

In long-sightedness, or hyperopia, the eye is slightly too short, so close-up things are harder to focus on. Lenses thicker in the middle help. In astigmatism, the cornea is curved more in one direction than the other, a bit like the surface of a rugby ball or an American football instead of a round ball. Some lines then look sharper than others, and glasses with specially shaped lenses correct it.

After about the age of 40, almost everyone's lens gets stiffer. That's why many grandparents hold menus at arm's length and need reading glasses.

The first glasses were made in northern Italy around 1286. A friar from Pisa, preaching in Florence in 1306, said that the art of making them had been discovered less than 20 years earlier. Those early glasses used [[@lenses-glasses|lenses]] thicker in the middle, so they helped older people read. Lenses for short-sighted people appeared in the 1400s.

Lens-making skill also led to [[@telescopes-make|telescopes]]. In 1609, [[@galileo|Galileo]] built his own and turned it to the sky.

Short-sightedness has become much more common in recent decades, especially in cities. In parts of East Asia, the large majority of young adults are now short-sighted. A 2016 study estimated that about half of the world's population could be myopic by 2050.

[[gene|Genes]] play a part, since short-sighted parents are more likely to have short-sighted children. But the fast rise points to the way children live. Studies, including school trials in China and Taiwan, suggest that spending more time outdoors in daylight lowers children's risk. Long hours of close-up work, such as reading and [[@screen-time|screens]], may add to it.

If the board looks blurry or you often squint or get headaches, tell a parent or teacher. An eye test is quick and painless, and glasses can make an immediate difference.

text: For thousands of years, farmers judged their fields by eye and by hand. Now many also use machines that measure. Soil [[sensor|sensors]] report how wet the ground is. [[@satellites-help|Satellites]] and drones photograph crops and spot sick patches before people can. Tractors guided by GPS drive in perfectly straight lines. Phone apps tell farmers tomorrow's weather and today's prices.

The big idea is called precision farming. Instead of giving a whole field the same water, [[fertiliser|fertiliser]] and [[pesticide|pesticide]], you give each patch only what it needs. That saves money and water, and keeps extra chemicals out of rivers.

st.prompt: A farmer has a big field. A soil sensor shows one corner is dry and the rest is fine. What does precision farming suggest?

options.t: Water only the dry corner
Water the whole field a bit extra, just in case
Wait until the whole field is dry

st.reveal: The idea is to treat each patch according to what it needs. Watering only the dry corner saves water, electricity for the pump, and money, and stops the rest of the field from getting soggy.

src: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, digital agriculture.
Government of India, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Soil Health Card scheme.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, precision agriculture.

d.try: Plant a few seeds in two cups of soil. Water one cup only when you poke your finger in and the soil feels dry. Water the other the same amount every day whether it needs it or not. Watch which seedlings do better over two weeks, and how much water each cup used.
myth: Farming technology is only for huge, rich farms.

Some machines are expensive, but many tools reach small farmers too. In India, farmers can rent machines from shared hiring centres, get weather alerts and crop prices on basic phones, and hire drone pilots by the hour.
facts: giving each patch of field only what it needs
drones, soil sensors, satellites, GPS tractors, phone apps
plan for 15,000 drones for women's self-help groups (announced 2023)
can cut water use sharply compared with flooding fields

sec.t:
Small sensors pushed into the soil can measure moisture and temperature and send the readings to a phone. This is part of the [[@internet-of-things|internet of things]], where ordinary objects are connected to the internet. A farmer can switch on a water pump from a phone, or get a warning before frost.

Drip [[irrigation|irrigation]] goes with this. Thin pipes carry water drop by drop to the base of each plant instead of flooding the whole field. It can save a large share of the water, which matters in places where the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] fails or wells are running low.

On large farms in the United States, Canada and Australia, many tractors use GPS to steer. The driver turns at the end of the field, and the tractor follows straight rows within a few centimetres. Some combine harvesters map how much grain each part of the field produced, so next year's seed and fertiliser can be adjusted patch by patch. Companies are now testing tractors that work with nobody in the cab at all.

India's farms are mostly much smaller. The average holding is about one hectare, and many families farm less than that. A giant machine makes no sense on a plot you can walk across in two minutes. So Indian technology often looks different: apps, rented machines and shared drones rather than giant self-driving harvesters.

In the 1960s, the [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]] gave Indian farmers new seeds, fertilisers and irrigation, and grain harvests jumped. It also left some soils tired and some water tables falling. Smart farming tries to keep yields high while using less.

There are worries too. Machines and data can be expensive, and some farmers ask who owns the information collected from their fields. In places with weak mobile signal, an app is not much use. Experts say the technology helps most when it is cheap, simple and explained by people farmers already trust.

Since 2015, India's Soil Health Card scheme has tested farm soil and told farmers which [[nutrient|nutrients]] their land is short of. The tools are new, but the questions are the ones [[@jobs-farmer|farmers]] have always asked: when will it rain, what does this soil need, and what will my crop sell for?

text: Around 321 BCE, a young man named Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the powerful Nanda kings of Magadha, in today's [[@bihar-history|Bihar]]. According to tradition, he was guided by a sharp teacher called [[@chanakya|Chanakya]].

Chandragupta then pushed west, taking land left behind by [[@alexander-india|Alexander the Great]]'s army. His son Bindusara and grandson [[@ashoka|Ashoka]] went further. At its biggest, the [[empire|empire]] stretched from Afghanistan to Bengal and deep into the south. It held together through a strong army, a large staff of officials, spies, taxes and good roads. For the first time, most of the [[subcontinent|subcontinent]] answered to one ruler.

st.prompt: What did the Greek ambassador Megasthenes say the walls of Pataliputra were made of?

options.t: Wood
Marble
Bronze

st.reveal: Megasthenes described a huge wall of wooden timbers with gates and towers. Archaeologists in Patna have since found long lines of wooden beams buried in the ground, just as he described.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mauryan empire.
Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961).
Archaeological Survey of India, Kumhrar excavations.
n.certNote: We have only a few sources for this period. Stone inscriptions are reliable, but the Greek accounts survive only as quotations, and the date of the Arthashastra is debated.

d.try: Draw a map of India and mark the places you or your family have lived or visited. Then shade in the area the Mauryas ruled, using an atlas or a book. Count how many of your places would have been inside the empire.
myth: India was always one country, and the Mauryas simply ruled it.
Before the Mauryas, the subcontinent was split into many kingdoms and republics. The Mauryas were the first to bring most of it under one ruler, and even they never ruled the far south.
facts: the Lion Capital, India's national emblem

sec.t:
Pataliputra stood where Patna is today, beside [[@rivers-himalaya|the Ganga]]. Megasthenes said it was enormous, with a wooden wall full of towers and gates, and a wide moat around it.

That sounds like a traveller's tall tale, yet excavations at Patna have uncovered lines of heavy wooden beams in the ground. At Kumhrar, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] also found the remains of a great hall with polished stone pillars. Wood rots, so most of the city is gone. The fact that any of it survived in damp earth for over 2,000 years is lucky.

Ruling so much land took organisation. The empire was divided into provinces, often run by princes. Officials measured fields, collected taxes, managed mines and forests, and kept roads in repair. A great royal road linked the northwest to Pataliputra, along much the same line as the later Grand Trunk Road.

A [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] book called the *Arthashastra*, linked by tradition to Chanakya, explains how a king should govern. It covers spies, prices, punishments, [[famine|famine]] relief and war. Historians use it with care, because parts of it were probably written later.

sec.h: A changed king and a lasting emblem
sec.t:
Chandragupta did not stay on the throne to old age. Jain tradition says he gave it up, became a monk and went south to Shravanabelagola in Karnataka.

The most famous Mauryan, Ashoka, turned away from war after a bloody conquest and spread messages carved on rocks and pillars. One of his pillars at Sarnath was topped by four lions sitting back to back. In 1950, India made that Lion Capital its [[@national-symbols|national emblem]]. You can see it on every rupee note.

After Ashoka died around 232 BCE, the empire shrank under weaker rulers. Around 185 BCE, the last Mauryan king, Brihadratha, was killed by his own general, Pushyamitra Shunga, who started a new [[dynasty|dynasty]].

The empire broke into smaller kingdoms again. But the idea that one government could hold together this huge and varied land had been tested, and it would return under the [[@gupta-golden-age|Guptas]], the [[@mughals|Mughals]] and modern India.

text: The Kremlin is a walled [[fortress|fortress]] in the centre of Moscow, the capital of Russia. "Kremlin" is an old Russian word for a citadel, the fortified heart of a town. Inside its red-brick walls are palaces, cathedrals, government buildings, museums and gardens.

For centuries it was the home of the tsars, Russia's emperors. Later it became the seat of the Soviet government. Today it is the official residence of the president of Russia, and part of it is a museum open to visitors. When news reports say "the Kremlin said", they mean the Russian government, much as "the White House" stands for the US president's office.

st.prompt: The colourful onion-domed church often shown in photos of Moscow is St Basil's Cathedral. Where is it?

options.t: Just outside the Kremlin walls, on Red Square
In the very centre of the Kremlin
In St Petersburg, far from Moscow

st.reveal: St Basil's stands at the end of Red Square, outside the Kremlin walls. Inside the walls are other cathedrals, with golden domes, where tsars were crowned and buried.

src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Kremlin and Red Square, Moscow.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kremlin.
Moscow Kremlin Museums, official site.

d.try: Draw a map of a fortress on squared paper. Give it walls, at least five towers and two gates. Then mark where you would put a palace, a church and a store of food, and explain to someone why you chose each spot.
myth: There is only one kremlin, in Moscow.
The word kremlin means a fortress in the middle of a town. Many old Russian cities have one, including Novgorod, Kazan and Nizhny Novgorod. Moscow's is simply the most famous.
facts: the centre of Moscow, Russia, beside Red Square
UNESCO World Heritage Site (with Red Square)

sec.h: From wooden fort to red walls
sec.t:
A wooden fort stood on this hill above the Moscow River by the 1150s. Over time it was rebuilt with oak walls, then white limestone. Moscow's rulers, the grand princes, grew more powerful and wanted something grander.

In the 1480s and 1490s, Grand Prince Ivan III hired architects from Italy. They built the red-brick walls and towers that stand today. The walls run for about 2.2 km, are up to 19 metres high in places and have 20 towers. The notched tops of the walls, shaped like swallowtails, look like those on castles in northern Italy.

In 1712, the tsar Peter the Great moved Russia's capital to his new city of St Petersburg. The Kremlin stayed important, and new tsars still came to Moscow to be crowned there.

In 1812, the French emperor [[@napoleon|Napoleon]] captured Moscow. Much of the city burned, and when his army retreated, it tried to blow up parts of the Kremlin. Several towers and walls were damaged but later rebuilt.

After the Russian Revolution of 1917, the new communist government moved the capital back to Moscow and set up in the Kremlin. Some churches inside were knocked down in the 1920s and 1930s. Red stars, lit from inside, were put on top of five towers in the 1930s, replacing the double-headed eagles of the tsars. They still shine at night today.

Just outside the eastern wall is Red Square, a huge open space where parades are held. "Red" here comes from an old Russian word that also meant "beautiful". At one end stands St Basil's Cathedral, with its swirling, colourful onion domes, built in the 1550s.

During the [[@cold-war|Cold War]], the Kremlin was the centre of the Soviet Union, the rival of the United States. People in the West used "the Kremlin" as shorthand for Soviet leaders. Its parades of soldiers and missiles across Red Square were watched closely around the world.

Today, visitors can walk through parts of the Kremlin and visit its cathedrals and museums. The Armoury Chamber holds crowns, thrones, carriages and jewelled Easter eggs made by the Fabergé company for the tsars.

Like the [[@red-fort|Red Fort]] in Delhi or the [[@forbidden-city|Forbidden City]] in Beijing, the Kremlin is a fortress-palace that has seen several kinds of rulers come and go.
